claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated starting alloy has high strength.
The untreated starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal phase or lamellar boundaries cause local stress concentrations, microcrack initiation, and limited ductility in the untreated alloy.
A controlled annealing treatment can trigger atomic segregation at lamellar interfaces.
Annealing-induced segregation will form ultrathin interfacial complexions at the lamellar boundaries.
The resulting interfacial complexions will be ductile intergranular films.
Interfacial complexions will reduce the impedance to dislocation motion across lamellar interfaces and promote smoother dislocation transmission.
Improved dislocation transmission will prevent dislocation accumulation and reduce local stress concentration.
Reducing interfacial stress concentration will delay microcrack nucleation.
The treatment will significantly increase room-temperature tensile elongation relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will maintain or slightly increase yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Lamellar structures that permit dislocations to shear across coherent interfaces can alleviate local stress concentration and avoid cracking during deformation.
A fine lamellar eutectic structure containing alternating FCC and B2 phases can exhibit both high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature.
Excessive annealing temperature or duration may cause phase changes or coarsening that compromise strength.
The proposed benefit is intended to apply under room-temperature tensile loading and ambient service conditions.
